A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sparse-imagination research. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite substantial expansion and reorganization in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation success rates, planning times, token-selection comparisons, probing experiments and robustness analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds LIBERO, Meta-World and physical-robot evaluations, together with new ablations and failure analyses.

M1.justification: The original grouped-attention world model and prediction/planning losses remain. v2 substantially extends inference through SmolVLA-guided action-chunk selection (Sections 3.2 and 4.3), gradient-descent trajectory optimization (B.5), and variance-driven Ada-Rand/Ada-Inc dropout adaptation (B.6).

E1.justification: The six original simulation environments are retained. v2 adds LIBERO training suites and LIBERO-10 evaluation, Meta-World's 50 manipulation tasks, and physical SO-101 PickPlace and Drawer tasks with newly collected demonstrations (Section 4.3; Appendix A.1), substantially expanding task and deployment coverage.

E2.justification: The existing Full/CLS and token-selection comparator roster is retained, with SmolVLA without planning added as VLA-only (Table 3; Figure 5). Within existing benchmarks, LHS gains Granular and Rope comparisons, while STAR and Attention-WM gain Granular comparisons previously absent from v1 Table 3 (v2 Table 4).

E3.justification: New protocols introduce 50-step action chunks, task-specific candidate counts, 100 LIBERO trials, 15 trials per Meta-World task, and 10 trials per physical task. Added experiments vary encoders, optimization steps, planning horizon and frame skipping, and introduce LPIPS, coverage-entropy and blind-spot measurements. Original CEM defaults largely persist; the longer horizon is an added ablation.

E4.justification: Beyond retained probing, grouped-attention and noise analyses, v2 tests alternative encoders, hyperparameter sensitivity, gradient-based planning, adaptive sparsity and prediction quality. Component-level latency profiling and controlled blind-spot studies investigate where acceleration originates and why importance-based selection fails (Section 5; Appendices B.1 and B.5–B.9).

E5.justification: Both versions report 20 masks for nHSIC and five-run means and standard deviations for probing and grouped-attention prediction errors; their corresponding plots are retained. No new seed-count, confidence-interval or significance-testing practice is introduced. The adaptive planner's rollout variance is a control signal, rather than added uncertainty reporting for experimental results.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive policy-guided, physical-robot and ablation results, including 80% PickPlace and 70% Drawer success at 50% dropout (Figure 5). Existing results also change: Table 1's Wall Full/CLS scores move from 85.0/91.7% to 91.7/85.0%. Several Granular/Rope token-selection averages are revised between v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 4; these revisions do not establish same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: v2 defines cluster-retention entropy through retained-token frequencies over spatial clusters (A.7) and corrects the token-cost description from exponential to quadratic (Section 3.2). Existing loss equations, nHSIC definitions and Gaussian-noise assumptions remain; no new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The efficiency and random-sampling claims remain, but v2's abstract, contributions and conclusion explicitly extend demonstrated applicability to VLA-guided complex and physical-robot tasks. Identifying a fundamental blind-spot problem in importance-based selection also becomes a central contribution, beyond v1's comparative finding that random sampling performs competitively.

C2.justification: v2 develops a substantive blind-spot explanation involving static importance scores, lost action discrimination and unbiased coverage, extending v1's redundancy and grouped-training explanations. Limitations shift from simulation-only and DINO-focused validation toward encoder-quality dependence and task-dependent sparsity, with adaptive dropout presented as preliminary rather than universally superior.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds substantial reproduction information: new dataset sources and configurations, teleoperation procedures, physical-task evaluation positions, SmolVLA architecture and training hyperparameters, asynchronous execution settings, goal images and joint-state targets. LHS and cluster-retention calculations also receive implementation descriptions. Original world-model architecture and hardware disclosures largely remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for SmolVLA, LeRobot, LIBERO, Meta-World, MoCo-v3, DINOv3 and LPIPS, while removing the Kaelbling and Chefer references. The core DINO-WM and token-efficiency positioning remains, with a refined argument about the mismatch between static importance metrics and dynamic planning.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, experimental narrative, token-selection discussion and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Experiments and analysis are separated into Sections 4 and 5, earlier explanations are reorganized, planning details move into Appendix A.3, and the appendices gain clearer subdivisions and disclosure statements.

P2.justification: v2 adds performance–latency plots, blind-spot illustrations, physical-task goal images and rollout panels, plus tables for new benchmarks and analyses. Existing tables gain average columns and additional rows, and the environment montage expands. Earlier probing, noise and simulation-rollout figures are retained and relocated; these are not new evidence.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's explicit simulation-only and DINO-focused validation gaps through physical-robot experiments and alternative-encoder tests. Controlled failure analyses, hyperparameter checks and latency profiling also strengthen the explanations of robustness and efficiency. These gains outweigh reporting defects: physical evaluations use only 10 trials per task, Drawer test positions are described inconsistently in Section 4.3 and Appendix A.1, and Table 1's new Full/CLS averages do not reflect its revised Wall entries.
